newsitem.title: USA: US bond mkt rally said technical, despite tame CPI.
newsitem.headline: US bond mkt rally said technical, despite tame CPI.

text.p: Tuesday's U.S. Treasury market rally was deemed technical in nature and not a signal of a shift in monetary policy expectations, despite falling yields after a tame March consumer price index, experts said.

U.S. Treasuries rallied as much as one full point, with yields falling as much as 11 basis points after the Labor Department reported a 0.1-percent rise in the CPI for March, while the CPI excluding food and energy prices rose 0.2 percent. Both were below market expectations.
"This is not a change of psychology; this is more of a technical rally, a short-covering rally," said Neil DeSarno, head trader at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Corp.
The benign CPI report caught the market off guard, as players were said to have feared the worst, following strong producer price and retail sales reports on Friday.
Thus, the market continued to take on short positions, which required covering after the CPI surprise, traders said.
But the longer end of the curve has led the rally, especially the 10-year sector, which market participants said reflects a focus on technical factors over fundamentals.

"When it's a fundamental move, you see the front end leading the way and the curve flattens," said Patrick Dimick, Treasury market strategist at UBS Securities LLC. "Today, what we have seen is not a truly fundamental move, but economic statistics sparking a sizeable technical bounce."

Helping matters, Dimick said, was the June bond contract starting the session from a more favorable 107 level, rather than 106 1/2. The rally would have been "less pronounced" if the contract had begun lower, he said.

"When you see the long end lead (a rally) it's an obvious reach for duration and an obvious short-covering bid," he added. "I don't think enough people believe this data takes the Fed out of the game for the May (Federal Open Market Committee) meeting."

Indeed, by midday, 30-year yields were down nine basis points to 7.08 percent, while 10-year yields fell 11 basis points to 6.88 percent. In contrast, two-year yields were down eight basis points to 6.45 percent and bill rates fell between one and six basis points.

"I don't think this morning's report reduces chances of a tightening on May 20," said Marty Mauro, senior economist at Merrill Lynch & Co. "As long as forward-looking indicators ... are rising, then the Fed will be raising rates."
But the lack of retail buying posed a problem for the market, players said, citing massive short-covering and some swapping into 10-year notes against 10-year bunds.
"We have got to get some fresh buyers or we'll give back this gain," said William Sullivan, director of money markets reserach at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.
DeSarno noted that some dealers are setting up new shorts, so, "we may get another short-covering rally this afternoon."

Still, experts said they expected Tuesday's euphoria to fade, as the market faces new challenges in coming days from economic data and fresh supply. Bond yields look to rise close to 7.25 percent and two-year notes above 5.90 percent in the near-term.

CPI "marginally decreases the odds of a Fed move," Dimick said. "But the FOMC did tell us in their policy statement after tightening in March that it did so to cool down demand growth and today's data are irrelevant for the outlook for demand growth."
